title: Right-Side Out: How Vesicles Form and Signal

scenes.visual: Title card 'Right-Side Out: How Vesicles Form and Signal' in bold white type (36 pt) over the dark-slate world that is already fading in behind it: on the left, the curved edge of a donor B cell with a warm-gold plasma membrane (#F5C542), cool-cyan cytosol (#38BDF8), and coral surface ligands (#FB7185) gently bobbing; on the right, two target T cells waiting across a dark extracellular gap. Label 'Schematic' discreetly in the bottom-right corner.

scenes.tts: Can a tiny scrap of membrane from one cell switch on only a matching target cell? If that vesicle forms inside the sender, how does its signal end up facing outward? An immune case and a membrane trick answer both questions.
scenes.caption: Can a tiny scrap of membrane from one cell switch on only a matching target cell? If that vesicle forms inside the sender, how does its signal end up facing outward? An immune case and a membrane trick answer both questions.
scenes.visual: Title fades out cleanly; the carried split-frame world fills 70% of the frame height. Left side: donor B cell (warm-gold membrane, cyan cytosol). Right side: top target T cell with emerald-green matching receptors (#34D399) and bottom target T cell with muted-violet non-matching receptors (#A78BFA). A single tiny gold-ringed vesicle studded with coral ligands drifts slowly out of the B cell across the gap, pausing between the two T cells with a pulsing white '?' beside its outward-pointing coral heads. Keep gentle ambient drift on background fluid specks.
scenes.narration: Can a tiny scrap of membrane from one cell switch on only a matching target cell? If that vesicle forms inside the sender, how does its signal end up facing outward? An immune case and a membrane trick answer both questions.

scenes.tts: B cells release tiny membrane sacs called extracellular vesicles into the fluid around them. These vesicles display peptide-loaded M H C class two molecules on their outer surface. They switch on only the T cells whose receptor matches that peptide. Nothing enters the T cell.
scenes.caption: B cells release tiny membrane sacs called extracellular vesicles into the fluid around them. These vesicles display peptide-loaded MHC class II molecules on their outer surface. They switch on only the T cells whose receptor matches that peptide. Nothing enters the T cell.
scenes.visual: Label 'B cell' (28 pt) on left and 'Extracellular vesicles' (28 pt) above three drifting gold-ringed vesicles carrying cyan centres and outward-pointing coral MHC class II blocks holding tiny white peptide bars. As vesicles drift right, one docks its coral MHC-peptide onto the top T cell's emerald receptor; an emerald glow ripples along the top T cell membrane ('Matching T cell: active'). Another vesicle bumps the bottom T cell's violet receptor and drifts away with no glow ('Non-matching: silent'). Zoom briefly to the contact: the vesicle stays intact outside the T cell.
scenes.narration: B cells release tiny membrane sacs called extracellular vesicles into the fluid around them. These vesicles display peptide-loaded MHC class II molecules on their outer surface. They switch on only the T cells whose receptor matches that peptide. Nothing enters the T cell.

scenes.tts: Why would a protein on a vesicle made inside the cell point outward? Follow a receptor that starts on the cell surface, its coral head facing outside. First, the plasma membrane pinches inward by endocytosis to form an endosome. That first flip points the head into the endosome, a trapped pocket of outside fluid.
scenes.caption: Why would a protein on a vesicle made inside the cell point outward? Follow a receptor that starts on the cell surface, its coral head facing outside. First, the plasma membrane pinches inward by endocytosis to form an endosome. That first flip points the head into the endosome, a trapped pocket of outside fluid.
scenes.visual: Smooth camera zoom into a patch of the left donor cell's surface (a generic receptor, schematic) so its gold plasma membrane and cyan cytosol fill 75% of the frame. A bold coral receptor head sticks outward into the dark extracellular space, with its short tail in the cyan cytosol. As the narrator explains endocytosis, that patch of gold membrane smoothly dimples inward into the cyan cytosol and pinches shut into a large circular endosome filled with slate-blue lumen fluid (#475569). Label 'Endocytosis: flip 1' (28 pt). Track the coral receptor head clearly: it now points inward into the slate-blue endosome fluid.
scenes.narration: Why would a protein on a vesicle made inside the cell point outward? Follow a receptor that starts on the cell surface, its coral head facing outside. First, the plasma membrane pinches inward by endocytosis to form an endosome. That first flip points the head into the endosome, a trapped pocket of outside fluid.

scenes.tts: Next, the endosome membrane bulges into the endosome's own interior, away from the cytosol, forming small buds. Each bud fills with a drop of cytosol as it grows. Before it pinches off, predict where the coral receptor head ends up.
scenes.caption: Next, the endosome membrane bulges into the endosome's own interior, away from the cytosol, forming small buds. Each bud fills with a drop of cytosol as it grows. Before it pinches off, predict where the coral receptor head ends up.
scenes.visual: Zoom closer on the large slate-blue endosome surrounded by cyan cytosol. A small patch of its gold rim carrying the coral receptor pushes inward into the slate-blue lumen, drawing a tongue of cyan cytosol into the neck of the bud (label 'Inward bud: flip 2'). Just before the neck pinches off, motion slows to a gentle pulse. A clean high-contrast question banner appears at the top (30 pt): 'Where does the coral head end up?' Two glowing '?' markers pulse—one on the bud's outer surface and one inside its tiny cavity, as two possible places for the coral head.
scenes.narration: Next, the endosome membrane bulges into the endosome's own interior, away from the cytosol, forming small buds. Each bud fills with a drop of cytosol as it grows. Before it pinches off, predict where the coral receptor head ends up.

scenes.visual: Hold the zoomed endosome with the forming internal bud poised mid-pinch, the top question banner 'Where does the coral head end up?' visible, and the two '?' markers gently pulsing while a subtle progress bar glides across the bottom edge so the frame stays alive during the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: The second flip cancels the first one, so the coral head faces outward again as the bud pinches off. The cytosol stays sealed inside. Extracellular vesicles keep cell orientation: ligands face out, internal cargo stays sealed. A compartment packed with these buds is a multivesicular body.
scenes.caption: The second flip cancels the first one, so the coral head faces outward again as the bud pinches off. The cytosol stays sealed inside. Extracellular vesicles keep cell orientation: ligands face out, internal cargo stays sealed. A compartment packed with these buds is a multivesicular body.
scenes.visual: The question banner fades; the bud pinches shut into a complete small internal vesicle floating in the slate-blue lumen. The '?' on the outside transforms into 'Ligands face out' (coral, 28 pt) and the '?' inside transforms into 'Cytosol sealed inside' (cyan, 28 pt). Four more identical small gold-ringed, cyan-filled, coral-studded vesicles pinch off smoothly from the rim until the compartment is packed. Label the compartment 'Multivesicular body' (30 pt) as the small vesicles drift gently inside.
scenes.narration: The second flip cancels the first one, so the coral head faces outward again as the bud pinches off. The cytosol stays sealed inside. Extracellular vesicles keep cell orientation: ligands face out, internal cargo stays sealed. A compartment packed with these buds is a multivesicular body.

scenes.tts: Picture this multivesicular body as a sorting room with two doors. If it fuses with a lysosome, digestive enzymes break the internal vesicles down. If instead it moves to the surface and fuses with the plasma membrane, those vesicles spill outside intact. Those released vesicles are exosomes.
scenes.caption: Picture this multivesicular body as a sorting room with two doors. If it fuses with a lysosome, digestive enzymes break the internal vesicles down. If instead it moves to the surface and fuses with the plasma membrane, those vesicles spill outside intact. Those released vesicles are exosomes.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back inside the donor cell to show two animated paths branching from the multivesicular body ('Two exits'). Upper path: a copy of the multivesicular body glides toward a muted-violet sphere labelled 'Lysosome' (#A78BFA), fuses with it, and the small vesicles fragment and fade. Lower path: the main multivesicular body glides right to the warm-gold plasma membrane, fuses smoothly so its gold rim merges with the cell surface, and its intact gold-and-cyan internal vesicles drift outward into the extracellular gap. Label them 'Exosomes' (30 pt).
scenes.narration: Picture this multivesicular body as a sorting room with two doors. If it fuses with a lysosome, digestive enzymes break the internal vesicles down. If instead it moves to the surface and fuses with the plasma membrane, those vesicles spill outside intact. Those released vesicles are exosomes.

scenes.tts: Cells also release microvesicles by budding straight outward from the plasma membrane. That direct step also buds away from the cytosol, giving the exact same orientation. Because exosomes and microvesicles overlap in size and markers, call vesicles of unproven origin extracellular vesicles.
scenes.caption: Cells also release microvesicles by budding straight outward from the plasma membrane. That direct step also buds away from the cytosol, giving the exact same orientation. Because exosomes and microvesicles overlap in size and markers, call vesicles of unproven origin extracellular vesicles.
scenes.visual: Just above the fused multivesicular body on the same donor plasma membrane, a patch of warm-gold membrane with coral heads bulges straight outward into the extracellular gap, enclosing cyan cytosol, and pinches off ('Microvesicle'). Side by side in the gap, an exosome and a microvesicle drift together—identical gold outer rings, outward coral ligands, cyan interiors, and overlapping diameters (schematic). A soft bracket joins both with the bold label 'Extracellular vesicles' (30 pt).
scenes.narration: Cells also release microvesicles by budding straight outward from the plasma membrane. That direct step also buds away from the cytosol, giving the exact same orientation. Because exosomes and microvesicles overlap in size and markers, call vesicles of unproven origin extracellular vesicles.

scenes.tts: This right-side-out layout gives a vesicle three ways to act on a target cell. First, a surface ligand binds a target receptor directly, like the B cell vesicles. Second, the vesicle membrane can fuse with a target membrane and spill sealed cargo into the cytosol.
scenes.caption: This right-side-out layout gives a vesicle three ways to act on a target cell. First, a surface ligand binds a target receptor directly, like the B cell vesicles. Second, the vesicle membrane can fuse with a target membrane and spill sealed cargo into the cytosol.
scenes.visual: Pan smoothly right to the target cell membrane, dividing the right half of the frame into three stacked action lanes along the same cell edge (all using the identical gold/cyan/coral/emerald colour map, marked 'Schematic'). Lane 1 ('1. Surface ligand'): a coral-studded vesicle docks on an emerald receptor; emerald signalling ripples inward while the vesicle stays outside. Lane 2 ('2. Membrane fusion'): a vesicle's gold ring merges seamlessly into the target membrane (or an endosome membrane), releasing glowing cyan cargo dots into the target cytosol.
scenes.narration: This right-side-out layout gives a vesicle three ways to act on a target cell. First, a surface ligand binds a target receptor directly, like the B cell vesicles. Second, the vesicle membrane can fuse with a target membrane and spill sealed cargo into the cytosol.

scenes.tts: Third, the target cell can swallow the vesicle by endocytosis. Swallowing alone is not a signal, because swallowed cargo usually ends up in the lysosome. Swallowed internal cargo acts only if it escapes or is sensed along the way. Orientation decides what acts on contact and what stays sealed.
scenes.caption: Third, the target cell can swallow the vesicle by endocytosis. Swallowing alone is not a signal, because swallowed cargo usually ends up in the lysosome. scenes.visual: Lane 3 ('3. Uptake'): the target plasma membrane wraps around an intact gold-and-cyan vesicle and pulls it inside into a slate-blue endosome, which drifts toward a muted-violet lysosome ('Often degraded') with a faint dashed arrow showing a rare escape path into cytosol ('Rare escape or sensing'). In the final beat, Lanes 1–3 settle side by side with a subtle highlight pulsing on the outward coral ligands in Lane 1 versus the membrane-enclosed cyan dots in Lanes 2 and 3.

scenes.visual: Clean dark-slate end card with one single centred line in crisp white type (32 pt), nothing underneath it, over a faint slowly drifting gold-and-cyan vesicle outline: 'Extracellular vesicles keep cell orientation: ligands face out, internal cargo stays sealed.'
